summary: Under the five equal Crown crests, Professor Corven opens the course with one question: five settlements lose the corridors on the same day; which one survives?
panelPlan: Tall opening view of cadets crossing the Crown Gallery beneath five equal crests and the larger Fleet constellation.
Corven waits beside the gallery threshold while traffic and cadets continue around her.
The five students slow as a historical corridor map appears on the wall display.
Close on the map breaking into five isolated points.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: REX FLEET ACADEMY: DOCTRINE OF MANY CROWNS

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: ISSUE 1 — FIVE ANSWERS

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Five settlements lose the corridors on the same day.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: No relief. No messages. No certainty that anyone else still exists.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Which one survives?

directionInline: The opening should feel like ordinary Academy life passing through monumental history. The five crests are equal in scale and subordinate to the shared Fleet visual grammar; do not stage them as five rival school houses.

summary: In seminar, Corven gives the five settlements identical starting conditions; the cadets immediately choose different priorities and expose different assumptions.
panelPlan: Five identical settlement models hover over the central table.
Bex checks supply figures while Tali expands the communications layer.
Kez points toward an approaching threat marker.
Emil studies the blank authority chart.
Corven watches rather than correcting them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Same population. Same stores. Same damage. Same bad information.

dialogueInline.speaker: Bex
dialogueInline.text: Then count the food before you do anything clever.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tali
dialogueInline.text: No. Rebuild signal first. You cannot allocate what you cannot see.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: If that contact is hostile, you can count the food after they take it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: Who is authorized to decide any of this?

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: You gave us identical settlements and five different emergencies.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: I gave you one emergency.

directionInline: The five settlement models must look materially identical at first. The difference comes from what each cadet chooses to foreground, not from pre-labeled Crown symbolism.

summary: Corven reframes the exercise: the question is not which ideology wins, but what each student would save first when everything cannot be saved at once.
panelPlan: Corven collapses the five models into one damaged settlement.
A ring of icons appears: records, beacon, authority seal, defense craft, convoy shield.
The students' hands hover over different icons.
Corven leaves all five icons lit.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: You're all answering a different question.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: You asked which one survives.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: And you heard: which one fights best.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Tali heard: which one coordinates. Bex heard: which one preserves resources. Emil heard: who can act. Nara heard: who pays.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: What did you mean?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: What do you save first when you cannot save everything at once?

directionInline: Do not map each cadet permanently to a Crown. This page exposes habits of attention, not house membership or personality sorting.

summary: The class enters the archive theater; Corven warns that the coming people are reconstructed from records and testimony, not literal Crown founders or saints.
panelPlan: Physical archive drawers open beside the projection table.
Corven places five worn source markers around the table.
Historical images bloom as incomplete layers, with visible gaps and conflicting annotations.
The room darkens until the first reconstruction surrounds the class.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: One rule before we begin.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: These are reconstructions: manifests, logs, testimony, later commentary.

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: Not the founders?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: There were no Crowns yet.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: If a lesson needs saints, it is probably hiding something.

directionInline: Make source uncertainty visible in the archive interface. Historical sequences are evidence-based dramatizations, not objective omniscient flashbacks.

summary: In the first reconstruction, archive keeper Iona Pell chooses to inventory and duplicate records while a damaged settlement demands immediate distribution.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — ISOLATED SETTLEMENT STOREHOUSE — FIRST WINTER AFTER THE SHATTERING
panelPlan: A damaged storehouse crowded with ration crates, paper ledgers and anxious residents.
Iona seals one ledger in a fireproof box while another clerk copies it by hand.
People outside pound on a distribution gate.
Iona discovers three crates whose labels no longer match the surviving manifest.

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: Nothing leaves until we know what is here.

dialogueInline.speaker: Resident
dialogueInline.text: We know what is here. Food.

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: We know what the boxes say.

dialogueInline.speaker: Resident
dialogueInline.text: People are hungry now.

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: Then we cannot afford to lose tomorrow inside a bad count.

directionInline: No mature Aurelian symbols. The proto-Aurelian idea must emerge from behavior: record, continuity and guardianship under material pressure.

summary: Iona's insistence on records looks cruel until the audit reveals seed grain and medical reserves that would have been consumed as ordinary rations.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — STOREHOUSE AUDIT FLOOR — LATER
panelPlan: Crates opened across the floor under portable lamps.
A clerk holds up sealed seed packets from a mislabeled ration crate.
Iona compares two conflicting manifests.
An angry resident sees medical cold packs in another wrongly marked box.
The distribution gate finally opens with corrected categories.

dialogueInline.speaker: Clerk
dialogueInline.text: This was marked meal stock.

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: It is next year's crop.

dialogueInline.speaker: Resident
dialogueInline.text: You made us wait for labels?

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: I made you wait because labels were wrong.

dialogueInline.speaker: Iona
dialogueInline.text: Eat the seed tonight and the ledger will look very clean when we starve.

directionInline: The scene must not vindicate bureaucracy in the abstract. The records matter because they reveal concrete food, seed and medicine that human memory under crisis misclassified.

summary: The settlement reaches spring with seed and kinship records intact, but the class sees the price of preservation: delays, resentment and people who left rather than wait.
panelPlan: Projection shows spring planting beside preserved family and medical records.
A second layer shows names of residents who departed during the winter.
Kez gestures at the departure list.
Bex touches the seed inventory.
Corven keeps both layers visible.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: So the lesson is paperwork wins?

dialogueInline.speaker: Bex
dialogueInline.text: The seed wins.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: And twenty-three people left before spring.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Guardianship preserved what panic could spend in a week.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: It also taught later Aurelian institutions how easily preservation can become a veto.

directionInline: Keep the success and cost on screen together. Do not let the page visually declare Aurelian correct or foolish.

summary: The second reconstruction follows signal coordinator Cal Rhyse building a beacon-and-routing network because isolated docks cannot share scarce ships or warnings.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — PATCHED SIGNAL TOWER AND DOCK NETWORK — SECOND YEAR AFTER THE SHATTERING
panelPlan: Several disconnected dock feeds flicker across Cal's improvised signal station.
Technicians raise a crude beacon mast outside.
Cal draws one shared route board connecting food, fuel and medical requests.
The first coordinated convoy icons begin moving.

dialogueInline.speaker: Technician
dialogueInline.text: North Dock wants the tug back.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: South Dock has oxygen for six hours.

dialogueInline.speaker: Technician
dialogueInline.text: They cannot see each other.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: Then we become the part that sees both.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: One board. One clock. Every ship reports.

directionInline: No mature Cerulean uniforms. The proto-Cerulean idea is a shared operational picture built out of desperate local systems.

summary: Coordination becomes authority when Cal refuses a local dock's demand to keep its tug, because the network needs it elsewhere.
panelPlan: North Dock supervisor fills one cracked screen, furious.
Cal's board shows the tug as the only craft able to reach South Dock in time.
A local crowd watches the argument from behind Cal.
Cal moves the tug marker despite the supervisor's objection.

dialogueInline.speaker: North Dock
dialogueInline.text: That tug is ours.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: It was yours yesterday.

dialogueInline.speaker: North Dock
dialogueInline.text: We lose heat if it leaves.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: South loses air if it stays.

dialogueInline.speaker: North Dock
dialogueInline.text: You do not live here.

dialogueInline.speaker: Cal
dialogueInline.text: No. I have to see farther than here.

directionInline: Cal's logic is defensible and painful. The page should make North Dock's local claim concrete rather than framing them as selfish.

summary: A cascading failure proves the value of the beacon network, but one damaged local station is sacrificed to preserve the larger route web.
panelPlan: Projection shows coordinated reroutes preventing a chain collision during a beacon outage.
One peripheral station drops dark while the main network stabilizes.
Tali studies the saved-route count.
Nara studies the dark station.
Corven overlays both outcomes on the same map.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tali
dialogueInline.text: Without the network, they lose four docks.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: With it, they choose one.

dialogueInline.speaker: Bex
dialogueInline.text: That is still better.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Usually.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Cerulean thought begins with a true observation: separated systems die because nobody can see the whole.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Its danger begins when seeing the whole becomes permission to own every part.

directionInline: The saved docks and sacrificed station must be visually simultaneous. Tali's technical admiration should not erase the local loss.

summary: The third reconstruction reaches a famine council that cannot agree; emergency steward Maera Quill takes temporary authority because indecision is consuming the remaining stores.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — CIVIC HALL DURING FAMINE — THIRD YEAR AFTER THE SHATTERING
panelPlan: A civic table covered with empty ration bowls and competing allocation proposals.
Council members argue while a public queue grows beyond the doors.
Maera lifts the plain emergency seal from the center of the table.
She closes the debate and orders the storehouse opened under ration control.

dialogueInline.speaker: Councilor
dialogueInline.text: We need another vote.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: We voted yesterday.

dialogueInline.speaker: Councilor
dialogueInline.text: There was no majority.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: There will be no majority after three more days without bread.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: Record my order. Record my name. Open the stores.

directionInline: No mature Ember red faction coding. The proto-Ember idea is visible in taking responsibility and accepting that the order must be attributable, not in theatrical fire imagery.

summary: Maera's emergency rule requisitions private reserves and standardizes rations, saving the public supply while making coercion unmistakable.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — PRIVATE WAREHOUSE / PUBLIC RATION LINE — DAYS LATER
panelPlan: Civic workers inventory a private warehouse under Maera's signed order.
The warehouse owner confronts her beside sealed luxury stores.
Public ration lines move under a new standardized allocation board.
Maera signs responsibility for the requisition in the same ledger.

dialogueInline.speaker: Warehouse Owner
dialogueInline.text: You cannot take this because you found a seal.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: I am taking it because people are starving.

dialogueInline.speaker: Warehouse Owner
dialogueInline.text: And when this is over?

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: Then you bring this order to me.

dialogueInline.speaker: Warehouse Owner
dialogueInline.text: If you still answer to anyone.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: Write that down too.

directionInline: Maera is neither villain nor savior. Show both the real hoarded surplus and the frightening fact that one office can now seize it.

summary: The famine eases, but Maera keeps the emergency seal because unrest remains; the class identifies the Ember truth and its self-perpetuating danger.
panelPlan: Projection shows full ration shelves returning months later.
A council member reaches for the emergency seal; Maera keeps it in her palm.
The image freezes on that hand.
Emil and Nara study the same frozen frame from different sides.

dialogueInline.speaker: Councilor
dialogueInline.text: The ration emergency is over.

dialogueInline.speaker: Maera
dialogueInline.text: The riots are not.

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: She saved them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: And now she has a reason to keep saving them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Ember remembers that authority can be a burden somebody must carry.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: It also remembers, less comfortably, that emergency authority can always find another emergency.

directionInline: The frozen emergency seal is the page's visual thesis. Avoid overt tyrant imagery; the danger is institutional continuation after a justified intervention.

summary: The fourth reconstruction presents a convoy trapped behind a raider screen; Dax Renner argues that waiting for perfect information will let the food run out.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — PATCHED DEFENSE CUTTER ABOVE A BLOCKADED SETTLEMENT
panelPlan: Improvised defense cutter bridge with a sparse hostile screen between the convoy and settlement.
Fuel and food clocks tick down beside uncertain enemy counts.
Other captains argue over comms.
Dax draws a narrow attack vector through the screen.

dialogueInline.speaker: Other Captain
dialogueInline.text: We do not know how many are behind them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: We know how much food is behind us.

dialogueInline.speaker: Other Captain
dialogueInline.text: Wait for another pass.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: Every pass is a decision.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: If waiting spends the thing we came to save, waiting is not caution.

directionInline: No mature Tempest heraldry. The proto-Tempest idea is that delay has an operational cost measurable in fuel, food and initiative.

summary: Dax's improvised strike breaks the blockade long enough for the convoy to pass, but the victory is visibly expensive.
panelPlan: Defense cutters accelerate through a narrow gap rather than forming a conventional line.
One hostile ship turns too late as the convoy surges behind the attack.
A friendly cutter takes a severe hit while still clearing the lane.
Food transports cross the threshold toward the settlement.
Dax watches one friendly transponder go dark.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: Convoy, move now.

dialogueInline.speaker: Pilot
dialogueInline.text: They are turning on us.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: Good. That means they are not turning on the grain.

dialogueInline.speaker: Pilot
dialogueInline.text: Kestrel Two is hit.

dialogueInline.speaker: Dax
dialogueInline.text: Mark them. Keep the lane open.

directionInline: The action should be legible and costly, not triumphant spectacle. The convoy passing and the friendly loss occur in the same visual beat.

summary: After the blockade run, Dax counts the dead instead of celebrating; the Academy debate turns on whether decisive force saved lives or normalized escalation.
panelPlan: Projection shows Dax walking a damaged hangar and reading a short casualty list.
Behind him, food containers unload into the settlement.
Kez looks at the successful convoy path.
Nara looks at the casualty list.
Corven overlays the clock that had been running down before the attack.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: If he waits, the colony starves.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: If every uncertain contact becomes a charge, somebody is always about to be attacked.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tali
dialogueInline.text: He was right about the clock.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: That is the Tempest truth.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Hesitation can kill.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: The danger is learning to call every uncertainty hesitation.

directionInline: Keep Dax's casualty counting sober. Tempest must emerge as a rational response to time pressure, not as a caricature of aggression.

summary: The fifth reconstruction follows convoy chief Sela Orr forming a protective shell around refugee transports when a nearby station also calls for help.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — CIVILIAN REFUGEE CONVOY IN DAMAGED CORRIDOR SPACE
panelPlan: Refugee transports cluster inside a ring of escorts.
A distress call flashes from a small station beyond the convoy route.
Sela plots an escort detachment toward the station.
The protection ring visibly thins on the model.

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: Station K-Three has two hundred twelve people.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: And the convoy?

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: Three thousand eight hundred.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: If I send two escorts, what happens to our aft screen?

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: It opens.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: Then we do not have two escorts.

directionInline: No mature Aegis green coding. The proto-Aegis idea is a literal protective formation and the arithmetic of responsibility.

summary: Sela refuses to break convoy integrity, holds the shield through an attack, and listens as the outside station's distress signal weakens.
settingText: HISTORICAL RECONSTRUCTION — REFUGEE CONVOY UNDER ATTACK — CONTINUOUS
panelPlan: Escorts close ranks as fire crosses the convoy edge.
A refugee transport with families visible through small ports remains inside the shield.
The distant station signal pulses on a side display.
Sela keeps the formation intact while the station signal drops to intermittent.
The convoy clears the danger zone.

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: K-Three is calling again.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: I hear them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: We could still turn one ship.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: And if this line breaks?

dialogueInline.speaker: Operator
dialogueInline.text: I know.

dialogueInline.speaker: Sela
dialogueInline.text: No. You know the number. I am the one saying no.

directionInline: Sela's refusal is protective responsibility, not indifference. Keep the distant distress signal present while the people inside the formation remain physically visible.

summary: The convoy reaches safety while the station's final status remains uncertain; the class names the Aegis dilemma: protection always creates an inside and an outside.
panelPlan: Projection shows thousands disembarking safely from the convoy.
A separate small icon for K-Three remains gray with status unknown.
Bex traces the convoy perimeter with a finger.
Emil looks toward the gray station marker.
Corven lets the boundary line remain after all other graphics fade.

dialogueInline.speaker: Bex
dialogueInline.text: If she breaks formation, she may lose everyone.

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: So protection is just choosing the larger number?

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: No. It is choosing who is inside your promise.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Aegis begins with duty: stand between danger and the vulnerable.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Its danger is forgetting that every shield draws a line.

directionInline: Do not resolve K-Three's fate on this page. The ethical pressure comes from an incomplete outcome, exactly as the historical actors experienced it.

summary: Corven restores the five settlement models and reveals the answer to her opening question: all five survived, and their survival stances later hardened into the Five Crowns.
panelPlan: The five original settlement models reappear around the class.
Each grows a thin historical line forward through decades of isolation.
Only at the far end do the five mature Crown crests appear.
The cadets realize every line continues.
Corven stands inside the five converging histories.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: Which one was it?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: All five.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tali
dialogueInline.text: You said one emergency.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: It was.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Five communities survived the same civilizational failure by learning different lessons from it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Isolation turned stances into institutions. Institutions into sovereignty. Later, we called them Crowns.

directionInline: This is the reveal. The historical lines should not imply these five case studies are the literal sole founders of each Crown; present them as representative archive cases feeding wider traditions.

summary: Back in seminar, Corven gives the cadets a mature Fleet command problem; instead of choosing one Crown answer, they begin asking the different questions each tradition preserves.
panelPlan: A mature Fleet scenario appears: unidentified contact, refugee convoy, failing beacon, incomplete legal authority and a closing corridor window.
Kez starts to point at the intercept vector, then stops.
Tali opens the sensor-confidence layer.
Bex opens convoy endurance; Emil opens authority; Nara marks civilians outside the current protection radius.
The table fills with questions rather than one highlighted solution.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Unknown contact. Failing beacon. Civilian convoy. Corridor window closes in eleven minutes.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: What happens if we wait?

dialogueInline.speaker: Tali
dialogueInline.text: What do we actually know?

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: Who can commit the convoy to a new route?

dialogueInline.speaker: Bex
dialogueInline.text: What breaks if we move it?

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: Who is outside the protection plan?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Better.

directionInline: The point is not that each student now 'belongs' to one Crown. They are learning to deliberately invoke multiple lenses before an irreversible decision.

summary: Corven states the doctrine plainly: the Crowns are preserved because no single survival truth is sufficient to govern civilization, and each becomes dangerous when universalized.
panelPlan: Corven turns off the tactical outcome and leaves only the five question markers.
The five Crown crests appear above them, equal and incomplete.
Emil looks from one crest to another.
Kez sits back, no longer trying to pick a winner.

dialogueInline.speaker: Emil
dialogueInline.text: So the doctrine says all five are right?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: No.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: It says no single truth of survival is sufficient to govern civilization.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: Then why preserve the Crowns at all?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Because each remembers a failure the others are capable of forgetting.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Many Crowns is not agreement. It is institutionalized incompleteness.

directionInline: Treat this as the intellectual center of the issue, but keep it visually simple and human. The doctrine is a constraint on certainty, not a mystical revelation.

summary: Walking back through the Crown Gallery, the cadets now read the crests as warnings as well as traditions; Corven gives them the practical duty the doctrine imposes.
panelPlan: The same gallery composition as Page 1, now seen from the opposite direction.
Cadets pass beneath each crest without grouping themselves by it.
Bex glances back at the Aegis shield motif; Kez at the Tempest storm-line; Tali at Cerulean beacon geometry.
Corven continues walking instead of stopping beneath any one emblem.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Your duty is not to defend a Crown.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: That sounds like something the Crowns would object to.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Frequently.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Your duty is to notice what everyone else has stopped seeing.

dialogueInline.speaker: Nara
dialogueInline.text: Including your own side.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Especially then.

directionInline: Mirror Page 1 without repeating it exactly. The change is interpretive: the same crests now read as disciplined dissent rather than five competing brands.

summary: The lesson ends overlooking active Fleet departures; Corven connects Many Crowns to Reach and Resolve and points the course toward the harder question of how the five surviving traditions learned to share one Fleet.
panelPlan: Cadets stop at a gallery window overlooking multiple Fleet ships departing in disciplined traffic.
The five crests reflect faintly in the glass but the ships share one Fleet visual grammar.
Kez looks toward Corven with one last question.
Final wide: ships separate into different routes while remaining part of the same traffic picture.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Reach tells us to reconnect what was broken.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Resolve tells us what we owe the people who survived it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Many Crowns tells us not to mistake one answer for all of them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kez
dialogueInline.text: And when the five answers contradict each other?

dialogueInline.speaker: Corven
dialogueInline.text: Tomorrow's lesson.

directionInline: End on active Fleet service rather than ceremony. The shared Fleet is the practical result of preserving disagreement inside a common purpose.
